paragraphs.heading: China's space station
paragraphs.text: Tiangong, a name meaning 'Heavenly Palace', is officially called the China Space Station in English. It is China's first space station with a permanent crew, and it has been in low Earth orbit since 2021. The China Manned Space Agency, or CMSA, runs it as the country's third station. It is one of two working stations today, alongside the International Space Station, or ISS, and the third modular station ever, after Mir and the ISS.

paragraphs.heading: How it came about
paragraphs.text: China formally asked to join the ISS program in 2007. Roscosmos and ESA backed working with China, but the Wolf Amendment, a US rule in force since 2011, barred Chinese participation. China launched its own lab, Tiangong-1, in 2011 and gained experience meeting and docking in orbit. Tiangong-2 followed in 2016, developing life support for longer stays and automatic docking and refuelling by Tianzhou, the craft used for cargo missions.

paragraphs.heading: Building the station
paragraphs.text: The core module, Tianhe, meaning 'Harmony of the Heavens', went up on 29 April 2021. Two lab modules followed in 2022: Wentian on 24 July and Mengtian on 31 October. All three were put together at the Wenchang Space Launch Site and launched from there on Long March 5B rockets. The station flies 340 to 450 km up at an inclination of 41°, and its pressurised volume of 340 m³ is slightly over a third of the ISS's. It has three robotic arms in use and three outside docking ports.

paragraphs.heading: Crews and visiting craft
paragraphs.text: Crews of three fly up on Shenzhou spacecraft for missions of about six months, and six people are aboard for a while during handovers. Shenzhou 12 brought the first crew in June 2021, and Shenzhou 15 finished the main assembly in November 2022 and began continuous occupation. Shenzhou 23 is the first try at a year-long mission. By May 2026, 21 craft had docked: 12 Shenzhou and 9 Tianzhou. Crews have made 24 spacewalks in Feitian suits, including the longest spacewalk ever, over 9 hours in 2024.

paragraphs.heading: Ion thrusters and a telescope
paragraphs.text: No crewed spacecraft before Tiangong used ion thrusters, which it relies on for station-keeping in orbit. Its communications are relayed through the Tianlian satellite network. A space telescope called Xuntian, meaning 'Touring the Heavens', is due to launch in 2027. It is designed to dock with the station from time to time for servicing and refuelling.

paragraphs.heading: Science aboard
paragraphs.text: The station is a lab for bioastronautics, microgravity, materials science and space technology. Researchers from 17 countries have taken part in its experiments, and Chinese teams have studied atomic clocks, Bose–Einstein condensates and the growing cycle of rice. In 2022 it completed the first full rice cycle in microgravity, from seed to harvest to planting the new seed. In May 2023, during Shenzhou 15, a new bacterial strain, Niallia tiangongensis, was found aboard. The first astronaut from Hong Kong flew to Tiangong, and China is also training astronauts from Macau and Pakistan.

paragraphs.heading: Names from myth
paragraphs.text: Early names in China's space program came mostly from the revolutionary history of the People's Republic. In recent decades they gave way to names with mythological or religious meaning, such as the Shenzhou crewed spacecraft, whose name means 'Divine Vessel'. Tiangong was reported to call up cultural and romantic images too. The launch of Tiangong-1 inspired love poetry, and media likened spacecraft docking to the folk tale of the cowherd and the weaver girl meeting again.
